title: The poets
hookLine: the surah's name, and the poets excepted who believe, do good and remember Allah (26:224–227)

lines: A POET COULD BE A WEAPON.
THE SURAH NAMED FOR THE POETS.
cards: In the Arabia the Prophet grew up in, the old histories describe the poet as no quiet figure with a notebook. A poet could be a weapon and a newspaper at once.
A tribe's poet praised his own people and mocked their rivals, and a sharp line could travel from camp to camp and stick to a family's name.
So when the Prophet began reciting the Qur'an, some opponents had a label ready: he's just a poet. Surah Ash-Shu'ara, named for the poets, ends by answering that.

teach.b: The surah's last verses don't flatter the poets of that time. Those who go astray follow them. They wander in every valley, chasing any mood or theme, and they say what they don't do.
Commentators read this as the answer to the label: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, they say, was not wandering, and did what he said. Elsewhere the Qur'an says plainly that it is not the word of a poet.

teach.h: EXCEPT THOSE WHO BELIEVE AND REMEMBER.
teach.b: Then, in the very last verse, a turn: except those who believe, and do good works, and remember God much, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. So the surah doesn't ban poetry.
It sorts it: words that wander, and words that remember. The exception had faces.

teach.h: HASSAN IBN THABIT ANSWERS IN VERSE.
teach.b: The Prophet had poets among his companions, Hassan ibn Thabit among them.
A report in Bukhari says the Prophet asked Hassan to answer the Quraysh's satires in verse, and prayed that God support him with the Holy Spirit, which Muslims understand as the angel Jibril.
Another hadith in Bukhari says some poetry is wisdom.

Later, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, a poet who had written against the Prophet, came and recited a well-known ode, and tradition says the Prophet gave him his own cloak; scholars discuss the strength of that story's chains.
From those beginnings grew a long tradition of praise poems for the Prophet, in Arabic and many other languages, sung at weddings and gatherings.

teach.h: WORDS THAT WANDER, WORDS THAT REMEMBER.
teach.b: The surah's test is simple: do the words remember God, and do the people saying them live them?

how: Muslims across the world sing and recite devotional poetry, from Arabic odes praising the Prophet to nasheeds and qawwali, while scholars hold that the Qur'an itself is not poetry.

games.q: the Quraysh are mocking the Prophet in verse, and the poems are spreading. you're Hassan ibn Thabit. what does the Prophet ask you to do?
o: find the poets and fight them.
games.why: a report in Bukhari says he asked Hassan to answer them, and prayed that God support him with the Holy Spirit.

practice: If you know a devotional poem by heart, a line of a nasheed, a verse someone once sang to you, a praise poem from your own language, let it play slowly in your mind and notice what it does to your breathing.
If none comes, sit with the surah's own words instead: those who believe, and remember God much. Notice which line you'd want to keep, and if you pray, say it as a prayer.

wordCard.voice: The poets. Ash-Shu'ara, the surah named for them, which turns away the poets who wander and keeps the ones who believe, do good and remember God much. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the poets; the singular, sha'ir, is tied in the lexicons to a root of perceiving.

carryVoice: Your line: words that remember. Poetry can wander, or it can remember. That's day five hundred nineteen.
